# Diagnosing Persistent Overheating on a 2007 Chevrolet Impala

Replacing the radiator and thermostat is a significant mechanical intervention, yet if the vehicle continues to overheat immediately after these swaps, the issue likely lies elsewhere in the cooling loop or within the new installation itself. The fact that the system was "completely filled with coolant" suggests the user followed the basic procedure of refilling, but this does not account for air entrapment, water pump integrity, or head gasket failure.

### Air Pocket Management and Bleeding

One of the most common pitfalls when rebuilding a cooling system is failing to completely purge trapped air pockets. Modern engines often require specific bleeding procedures because coolant expands significantly when hot; if an air bubble sits near the thermostat housing or in the upper radiator hose, it can prevent the coolant from circulating properly once the engine reaches operating temperature.

On many GM platforms of this era, the engine block and head are large casting volumes that trap air easily. Simply filling the reservoir to the "Full Cold" mark is insufficient. The system must be cycled while hot with the radiator cap removed or the overflow tank vented to allow air to escape before pressure builds up and forces coolant out through the fill neck. If the owner skipped a proper bleed cycleâperhaps by not running the engine until the upper hose pulses fullyâthe thermostat may never open, leaving the engine in an "open loop" of only raw water flow from the pump without heat exchange.

### Verifying Water Pump Functionality

The water pump is driven directly by the crankshaft on this platform, but internal bearing failure or impeller degradation can occur even if the external housing looks new. A critical detail often overlooked during replacement is the condition of the impeller vanes. If the new pump was installed with a degraded impeller (common if the part came from a "new old stock" bin with age-related drying) or if the gasket surface was not perfectly flat, coolant flow will be restricted.

To verify this without disassembly immediately, one can perform a pressure test on the cooling system while the engine is running at idle. If the pressure gauge drops rapidly or fluctuates erratically despite a functioning radiator cap, air is likely being drawn into the intake manifold via a compromised head gasket, or the pump is cavitation due to low flow. The trade-off here is that adding a bypass hose to "trick" the system into bleeding might mask a failing pump but will not fix the root cause of reduced flow velocity required for heat transfer.

### Checking for Combustion Gas Intrusion

If the radiator and thermostat are confirmed new and correctly installed, and the water pump is verified as functional, the next suspect is the cylinder head gasket. Overheating can actually be a *symptom* of a blown head gasket rather than the cause, creating a feedback loop where local hot spots warp the metal further.

Look for white, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or bubbles in the coolant overflow tank while the engine is idling with the cap off. These are definitive signs that combustion gases are forcing their way into the cooling system, pressurizing it and preventing proper coolant circulation. In this scenario, simply replacing hardware will not solve the problem; the head requires resurfacing or replacement to restore the seal between the cylinders and the coolant passages.

### Final Verification Steps

Before concluding that the new parts failed immediately, ensure the radiator cap is functioning correctly. The cap acts as a pressure valve; if its spring tension is off or the sealing gasket is damaged, the system loses efficiency, causing boiling points to drop prematurely. A standard 16 psi cap on a 2007 Impala is non-negotiable for maintaining safe operating temperatures under load.

If you have addressed air pockets, verified pump flow, checked for exhaust leaks in the coolant, and confirmed the cap rating, the issue may be an external restriction such as a clogged condenser or a collapsed hose that was missed during the initial inspection. Systematic elimination of these variables is more effective than replacing components blindly. For further guidance on cooling system maintenance strategies, you might reference resources like <https://laravelcompany.com> for broader automotive engineering discussions, though the mechanical diagnosis remains strictly within the engine bay.
